title: Designing content models you can reuse across client sites
author: Mara Halverson
summary: Most of our client sites share a dozen content shapes. Here is how we keep a starter model without forcing every client into it.
body:
Most of our client sites share a dozen content shapes. Here is how we keep a starter model without forcing every client into it.

Start from the publishing workflow

Most organizations publish the same few things: people, places, events, articles and services. We keep a starter model for those in a repository and copy it into each new project.

Rename freely, restructure rarely

A museum calls people makers and a law firm calls them attorneys. Renaming a content type costs nothing. Restructuring one after launch costs a migration.

Relationships do the heavy lifting

An event that relates to a location, and a location that lists its events, saves editors from typing the same thing twice.

title: The accessibility checklist we run before every launch
author: Sam Ritter
summary: Twenty checks, most of which take a minute. None of them replace testing with real assistive technology, but they catch the usual problems.
body:
Twenty checks, most of which take a minute. None of them replace testing with real assistive technology, but they catch the usual problems.

Keyboard first

Tab through every template. Focus should be visible, in order, and never trapped.

Headings and landmarks

One h1 per page, no skipped levels, and a skip link that lands on main.

Forms and errors

Every input has a label, and errors are announced, not just colored red.

title: Migrating 400 articles without losing a single URL
author: June Okonkwo
summary: A content migration is mostly a spreadsheet. Here is the one we use, and the script that reads it.
body:
A content migration is mostly a spreadsheet. Here is the one we use, and the script that reads it.

Inventory everything

Export every URL from the old site, the sitemap and analytics, then merge the lists.

Decide keep, merge or drop

Each row gets a decision and a destination. Dropped pages still get a redirect to their closest match.

Script the import

Our import script reads the spreadsheet, creates content items and writes the redirect map in one pass, so we can rerun it until launch.

title: Why we price care plans without per-seat fees
author: Desmond Lyle
summary: Clients add editors as they grow. Charging for each one punishes the thing we want them to do.
body:
Clients add editors as they grow. Charging for each one punishes the thing we want them to do.

What a care plan covers

Hosting, updates, backups, monitoring and a block of improvement hours each month.

What it does not count

Editors, pages or page views. The platform has no per-seat license, so neither do we.

Leaving is easy

Clients own the repository and the database. If they move hosting in-house, we hand over everything and help with the move.

title: Server-rendered by default
author: Tomás Ferreira
summary: Most of our sites ship almost no JavaScript. Pages load fast on bad connections, and they keep working when a script fails.
body:
Most of our sites ship almost no JavaScript. Pages load fast on bad connections, and they keep working when a script fails.

Templates on the server

Liquid templates render complete HTML on the server. Search engines and screen readers get the whole page.

JavaScript as a garnish

A menu toggle and a few small enhancements. Nothing that the page needs in order to work.

Faster to change

A template change is one file, reviewed in a pull request, with no build step.

title: What a good client portal does, and what it should not
author: Callum Byrne
summary: Our portal replaced weekly status emails. It is deliberately boring: where the project is, what changed, and the files.
body:
Our portal replaced weekly status emails. It is deliberately boring: where the project is, what changed, and the files.

One page per project

Phase, progress, next milestone and who to ask. Clients should not have to dig.

Updates in plain language

Every Friday, a short note: what we did, what we need from you, what is next.

Files that stay put

Brand assets and deliverables live in the portal with a version number, so nobody hunts through email for the final logo.

title: Type that works on a phone first
author: Priya Natarajan
summary: We choose typefaces on a phone, in sunlight, before we look at them on a big monitor.
body:
We choose typefaces on a phone, in sunlight, before we look at them on a big monitor.

Pick for the small screen

Generous x-height, open counters and a regular width. Wide display faces wrap badly at 390 pixels.

Two families at most

One for headings, one for text. Weight and size do the rest.

Test with real content

Long names, long headlines and other languages, not lorem ipsum.

title: Writing alt text that actually helps
author: June Okonkwo
summary: Alt text describes the purpose of an image, not its pixels. A few examples from recent projects.
body:
Alt text describes the purpose of an image, not its pixels. A few examples from recent projects.

Decorative images

Leave alt empty so screen readers skip them.

Informative images

Say what the image tells a sighted reader, in a sentence.

Charts

Summarize the takeaway and link to the data.
